title: First Friday Gallery Walk Opening Reception: Through my Own Eyes﻿ ﻿: black & white film photography by ﻿Jaime Sweany
location: Juniper Art Gallery,615 West Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47404, USA
description:
Juniper Art Gallery has not featured photography before, but Owner, Jaime Sweany, has often been asked if she is an artist and "Do you have any work here?" As some of you know, she's had photographs hanging in the gallery's restroom, and that's often gotten a giggle from the inquiring folk.

But seriously, before being a gallerist, Sweany was an avid photographer, concentrating mostly on portraiture due to her fascination with faces. She ran Illuminessence Photography from 1990-2005. After photo shoots, she spent countless hours in her dark room watching the magic happen as she developed her black & white film.

Sweany concentrated on both photography and hand-built ceramic artwork while attending Indiana University, receiving her B.A. in Studio Arts. She loved the fact that the two art forms she enjoyed the most were opposite. Ceramics felt like wild abandon, playing in the mud of creativity, and photography required that not a speck of dust was present in the darkroom, such drastically different work environments!

This exhibit, "Through My Own Eyes" includes many portraits from Sweany's 1990's body of work, "REAL: Beautiful Women." The culture of the day seemed to only appreciate the stereo-typical beauty of youth and left many women feeling unseen. This project highlighted the inner and the outer beauty of women of all ages, sizes, ethnicities, and demographics.

Note: none of the works in this exhibit are for purchase, but Ms. Sweany wishes to share her artwork with others while Juniper still serves as a platform.

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan Exhibition Opening
location: Gayle Karch Cook Center for Public Arts and Humanities,Cook Center for Public Arts and Humanities, 750 East Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA
description:
Join us for the opening of In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan, a new exhibition in the Process Gallery at the Gayle Karch Cook Center! Opening on September 4th, 5-8 pm, come check out the art and enjoy some light refreshments during our Gallery Walk hours. This exhibition will be up through December 4th, 2026.

In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan celebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural, August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan. Organized in partnership with Indiana University’s Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.

The exhibition brings together Qahar’s vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan’s history, traditions, and everyday beauty - with August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan, a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants’ voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.

Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.

title: Osamu James Nakagawa | Trace | Opening Reception
location: Pictura Gallery,202 South Rogers Street, Bloomington, IN 47404, USA
description:
This September, Pictura presents Trace, a new photographic series by longtime Bloomington treasure Osamu James Nakagawa, distinguished Professor of Photography at Indiana University. The project connects Nakagawa’s present day experience as a Japanese-American with past generations. In 2022, he began a 25,000 mile pilgrimage from Bloomington to visit the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps. Trace combines photographs taken at these sites with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.

Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. Trace seeks to reveal what can’t be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.

Trace opens at Pictura Gallery on Friday September 4th 5-8pm, and will be on view until October 30th.

title: Days and Nights in the Forest/Aranyer din ratri | Arthouse Now
location: Indiana University Cinema,1213 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47406, USA
description:
Desperate to flee Calcutta’s rat race, four friends drive to Palamu, one of India’s rural “tribal lands,” where they bribe a watchman into letting them stay at a guesthouse. Despite vowing to get away from it all, the crew soon mixes with the locals while simultaneously trying not to fall back into bad habits (aka booze, gambling, and girls). Filled with some of Ray’s most indelible characterizations and lavish images (shot by longtime cinematographer Soumendu Roy), Days and Nights in the Forest touches on masculine vulnerabilities and Indian class divisions with the graceful complexity of a master at his peak. [115 min; drama; Bengali with English subtitles]

Restored in 4K in 2025 by The Film Foundation’s World Cinema Project and Film Heritage Foundation in collaboration with Janus Films – The Criterion Collection at L’Immagine Ritrovata laboratory, from the original camera and sound negatives provided by Purnima Dutta and the magnetic track preserved by BFI National Archive. Funding provided by the Golden Globe Foundation. Special thanks to Wes Anderson and Sandip Ray.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: "Skills for Disagreeing Better" Braver Angels Workshop
description: This two-hour in-person workshop teaches better skills for sharing viewpoints in a way the other person might hear - even if they disagree - and to better understand the values and concerns of people who differ from you politically. Launched in 2016, Braver Angels is a non-profit bipartisan citizen's movement to unify America. By bringing Americans together into a working alliance, Braver Angels is building new ways to talk to one another, participate together in public life, and influence the direction of the nation. Indiana Braver Angels began in 2018 with the Red/Blue workshop in Bloomington. A local alliance started soon thereafter and is now leading weekly conversations. In this polarized time, we lack basic understanding of why people on the other political side hold their beliefs. We don't see them as they see themselves - their core values and central concerns - but instead as we choose to see them. We are tempted to regard our own side as principled and the other side as self-interested. When we try to communicate across this gap, we often lack the skills for listening carefully, looking for common ground, and sharing our perspectives in ways that connect rather than create more misunderstanding. By creating opportunities for meaningful discussions, Braver Angels works to dial down the heated rhetoric that gets in the way of real conversations and accurate understanding of our differences. The objective is not to push an agenda or change participant's minds, but rather to provide a safe place for deeper understanding. RSVP is requested at www.BraverAngels.org/indiana \(Promo Code "BRAVER" for free registration\) as seating is limited. \*\* This event is open to the media upon approval. Send requests to press@braverangels.org

title: Simply the Best: A Tribute to the Music of Tina Turner
location: Brown County Playhouse, 70 S. Van Buren St, Nashville, IN, 47448, United States
description:
How do you build the perfect performer? You would start with her voice. One that is beautiful, but strong. Mighty yet sensitive. It would be gritty, soulful, and unique. Then she would have looks that kill, and (of course) amazing hair. Her stage show would be entertaining, powerful and it would electrify the air. She would have charisma and charm. She’d perform rock, blues, soul, ballads and roof-raisers.
Well, we don’t need to build this perfect performer. She’s already been made and her name is Tina Turner! 
“Simply the Best: A Tribute to the music of Tina Turner” starring Jenn Cristy (national touring performer and former backing vocalist/instrumentalist for John Mellencamp). “Simply the Best” showcases the power and love for the stage that Tina projected over a 50 year career. Jenn Cristy perfectly embodies Tina’s transformative energy and spirit from the stage. 
Jenn has always felt a kinship with Tina, her music and her performing style. You’ll see why, as she dazzles in this amazing concert event. The show features hit songs such as Proud Mary, River Deep – Mountain High, What’s Love Got To Do With It, The Best, and many more. Jenn performs Tina like no other, and after you see all the great Tina songs along with an eclectic mix of other favorites, you’ll leave saying, ” That was…simply the best”.

description:
Take a chance to win ‘Painters Point’, a beautiful original oil painting generously donated by Guild Artist, Allen Hutton. Allen has achieved numerous awards and his art can be found in both private and corporate collections across the county.

The winner need not be present for the drawing.

title: Public Tour: Nature-inspired Art
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: The tour visits three floors of the museum, looking at a variety of nature-inspired artworks from global cultures, including nature-inspired photography in the featured exhibition The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection (https://artmuseum.indiana.edu/exhibitions/2026-08-29-photographic-reflex-marks-deprez.html).  This tour changes each time, based on what's on view. Additional tour highlights may include:from the forest of Papa New Guinea, an artwork made from natural materials, representing a leaf spirit, worn for a night dance  a treasured bowl that held kola nuts, for welcoming guests to an African palace  a sacred object from an indigenous culture (Maori), made for ocean voyages from a single tree that can live to be 1,000 years old  a large guard, with ancient origins, finely crafted, by a Kenyan artist, into an exquisite food storage container and later repaired  Hand-crafted bamboo baskets from Japan  Paintings of larkspurs, chrysanthemums, and more    Plus, look for signs of nature and discuss the influence of garden experiences on I.M. Pei's iconic architecture.  Each tour may vary slightly, depending on the tour guide.Know Before You GoAdmission and tours are free.Check in with Guest Services at least 5 minutes before the tour start time, to claim your reservation. At 1:25 p.m. any unclaimed spaces may be given to guests who are waiting for a space.Read about where to find us, where to park, accessibility, and museum guidelines.To save time at the lockers, avoid bringing backpacks or large bags.  When You ArriveCheck in with Guest Services staff on the first floor by 1:25 p.m.Store any backpacks or large bags. Lockers and coatrack are available.Do not touch artwork. Be mindful to keep all body parts – and anything you're carrying – at least 18" (a half meter) away from artwork.Photography is welcome, without flash or selfie stick.If you parked in the IMU parking lot, Guest Services can validate your parking voucher for a discount.    If this page says registration has closed, this means the waitlist is full.  To request this tour at another time for a group of 6-24 people, contact Laura at ematours@iu.edu (mailto:ematours@iu.edu).

title: T.C. Steele Centennial Exhibit
description:
On July 18th, be the first to see this once in a lifetime exhibition of Indiana’s premier Hoosier Master, Theodore Clement Steele.
Seventy paintings that span his revered career will fill the walls of the historic Brown County Art in memoriam of Steele’s passing in 1926 and the founding of the Gallery by the artists who followed him to Brown County.
Paintings come from private and public collections and have rarely been seen by the public. A full color catalogue features each painting and Steele’s extensive exhibition history. It’s a must have for both the patron and the educator. Copies are $25 but one will be included with each opening night reservation.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: T.C. Steele Centennial Exhibit
description:
On July 18th, be the first to see this once in a lifetime exhibition of Indiana’s premier Hoosier Master, Theodore Clement Steele.
Seventy paintings that span his revered career will fill the walls of the historic Brown County Art in memoriam of Steele’s passing in 1926 and the founding of the Gallery by the artists who followed him to Brown County.
Paintings come from private and public collections and have rarely been seen by the public. A full color catalogue features each painting and Steele’s extensive exhibition history. It’s a must have for both the patron and the educator. Copies are $25 but one will be included with each opening night reservation.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: I Ride
location: Sherwood Oaks Christian Church, 2700 E Rogers Rd, Bloomington, IN 47401, USA
description:
The iRide is a no drop ride with regroup points geared toward the rider wanting to push the pace a bit without being race oriented. 16-18mph avg on most rides. We typically follow the OWLS group route and add some extra miles/climbs in the second half of the route allowing folks to start out with us and if we are too fast they can drop back to the OWLS group. All interested in a brisker pace are welcome!

Non-members should sign up for a free trial membership of up to one month and sign a liability waiver before participating in a club ride. https://secure.getmeregistered.com/get_information.php?event_id=141883

title: OWLS -
location: Sherwood Oaks Christian Church, 2700 E Rogers Rd, Bloomington, IN 47401, USA
description: Non-members should sign up for a free trial membership, good for up to one month, and which includes electronically signing a liability waiver, prior to participation.The “Older, Wiser, and a Little Slower” group emphasizes moderate rides and a route planned in advance that is posted on the ride calendar. This is a no drop ride for a range of intermediate riders—it is not a beginner’s ride. Average pace is 12-15 mph which includes hills.  Regroup points are discussed in advance. Early season rides are shorter, and rides get longer as the season progresses. Peak season rides average 25–35 miles, depending on available daylight. Rides depart promptly at 5:45. Front and rear lights are encouraged. Questions? Contact Gail Morell.

title: It's On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop
description:
The It’s On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop is a 90-minute, audience-driven bystander intervention program that teaches students the skills needed to help in situations involving alcohol and drug use that could lead to a sexual assault. Students practice helping in real-life scenarios and discuss how alcohol and drug use influences a person’s ability to give and get consent to engage in sexual activity with another person.  


It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.  


Instructions:  


Those who arrive more than 5 minutes after the start time will NOT be allowed into the session and will need to attend a different session 


If this is your assigned workshop but you cannot attend it in its entirety, please RSVP for a different workshop. 


If you have concerns about attending due to personal experiences or need to request accommodations, please contact the office at itsonus@iu.edu. 


All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all IU students and other members of the Indiana University community.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

description: ICPSR (https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/home) is one of the largest archives for social and behavioral science data and, with over 28,000 studies, there might just be something for you! description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

title: Help Nepal: A Community Forum and Fundraiser for Nepali Flood Victims
location: The Cook Center in Maxwell Hall
description:
ACC is co-sponsoring this event with Nepali Student Association, Union Board and APA Staff & Faculty Council.
 
Join us for a special benefit gathering to support long-term relief and rebuilding efforts in Nepal. The event will take place on Wednesday, September 9, 2026, from 4:30 PM to 5:30 PM at the Maxwell Hall Cook Center. This gathering is co-sponsored by the Asian Culture Center, the Asian Pacific American Faculty and Staff Council, and the Nepali Student Association. (Online link will be posted soon!)


 
On August 26, 2026, a massive glacier collapse near the China–Nepal border triggered catastrophic flash floods and debris flows along the Trishuli River basin. The surge swept away entire towns, critical bridges, and essential border infrastructure, claiming over 1,200 lives and leaving thousands missing. Nearly 25 miles of road and 32 bridges were destroyed across steep, remote districts, making physical reconstruction a long and hazardous effort. The threat of repeat glacial- and landslide-triggered floods is high.
 
The September 9 gathering will feature personal perspectives from members of the IU Bloomington Nepali community alongside expert insights from Dr. Brian Yanites, an IU geologist specializing in landslides who has been closely monitoring the disaster. Volunteers will be available throughout the event to guide attendees on how to make direct monetary donations to relief efforts.
 
IU Bloomington shares a deep and lasting connection with Nepal. Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom brought global attention to the Himalayan nation through her seminal research on its community-managed resources, and IU students continue to visit Nepal through annual literary and cultural exchanges.
 
We hope you can join us in demonstrating our campus community's care and commitment to Nepal during this critical time.

Through archival footage, historic radio calls, interviews, and personal reflections, the documentary explores Fischer’s unlikely rise from a small-town Illinois upbringing to becoming one of the most recognizable voices in college sports.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: HIV/STI Testing
description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:
Write and work in solidarity with other IU scholars. We offer a silent work environment with coffee and natural light. The write-in is open to all graduate students (at any stage of their degree program).

 

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursday from 1-3pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

Co-sponsored by Writing Tutorial Services and the IU Libraries.

title: Exhibition Opening Reception for The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Thursday, September 10, 20264–6 p.m. Opening reception  Hors d'oeuvres and cash bar (4–6 p.m.)  First floor atrium  About The Photographic Reflex: The Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. Collection (https://artmuseum.indiana.edu/exhibitions/upcoming/_feature-exhibitions/2026-08-29-photographic-reflex-marks-deprez.html):  Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the IU Eskenazi Museum of Art from collectors Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. The exhibition features more than one hundred photographs by eighty artists, highlighting the breadth, power, and enduring impact of photographic expression.  Photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 reveal photography's dual role as both a tool for documentation and a vehicle for artistic exploration. Organized into five thematic sections—Play of Light, Industrial Eye, Photographic Figure, Witness to Conflict, and Impressed by Nature's Hand—the exhibition examines how photographers across disciplines have communicated ideas, recorded history, and shaped visual culture.  The exhibition includes works by many of the most influential figures in the medium, from Berenice Abbott, Alfred Stieglitz, Edward Steichen, and Henri Cartier-Bresson to contemporary artists such as Edward Burtynsky, Abelardo Morell, Susan Derges, and Vik Muniz.  A richly illustrated exhibition catalogue, featuring an interview with the collectors, will accompany The Photographic Reflex and will be available for purchase through the museum's Newkirk Café and Gift Shop.
source: Architecture + Design, Eskenazi Museum of Art, IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Eskenazi School of Art

title: Andy Smith, tuba/euphonium; Tomoko Kashiwagi, piano
description: Repertoire  Shostakovich/Atovmyan/McCourt: 'Waltz No. 2' from "Suite for variety orchestra" (c.1956?) Allen Vizzutti: Cascades (1980/2009)R. Schumann: Drei Romanzen, Op. 94 (1849)H. Eccles: Violin Sonata in G Minor (1720)Koetsier: Concertino, Op. 77 (1978/82)About the ArtistsAndy Smith was appointed by to the Lyric Opera of Chicago orchestra by Andrew Davis in January of 2012. He began performing with the group in September of that same year. Smith, from Amarillo, Texas, earned a Bachelor of Music degree from Texas Tech University, where he studied with Kevin Wass. He has also studied at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music with Daniel Perantoni. Prior to winning the Lyric Opera position, Smith was a highly sought after tubist in Texas, where he performed regularly with the Lubbock and Big Spring Symphonies. In addition to his duties in the pit, Smith has served as the principal tubist for the Grant Park Orchestra since 2018. He has also performed with many different orchestras in the Midwest including the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, the Detroit Symphony Orchestra, the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra, the Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra, and the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra. Smith is a Buffet Performing Artist. Smith is on the faculty of the DePaul School of Music.Tomoko Kashiwagi is visiting lecturer in music in chamber and collaborative music at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. Kashiwagi was previously associate professor of piano and collaborative piano and held the Emily J. McAllister Endowed Chair at the University of Arkansas, where she joined the faculty in 2012. She is also the founder of the Ozark Music Initiative, a nonprofit dedicated to building community through music. Her work has been supported by multiple Mid-America Arts Alliance grants. In 2025, she was inducted into the Steinway & Sons Music Teacher Hall of Fame in recognition of her commitment and passion as piano educator. She has presented multiple times at CollabFest, the conference of the International Keyboard Collaborative Arts Society. Maintaining an active performance career across the United States and internationally, Kashiwagi is dedicated to exploring a wide range of repertoire as both a performer and educator, with a particular passion for collaborative playing. She earned a Bachelor of Music, Master of Music, and Performer Diploma in Piano Performance from Indiana University. She later became the inaugural recipient of the Doctor of Musical Arts in Collaborative Piano degree from the University of Texas at Austin, where she studied with Anne Epperson, current chair of Jacobs' Department of Chamber and Collaborative Music.

description:
A long-term, hybrid in-person and online reading group in memory of our beloved friend, Joshua Clover inspired by Joshua’s understanding of communism, and social transformation. 

Our itinerary begins with Riot Strike Riot (Clover) and works backward through Chaos and Governance in the Modern World System (Arrighi and silver ), The Eclipse And Re-emergence Of The Communist Movement(Dauvé and Martin), The Arcana Of Reproduction (Fortunati, Trans Austin and Colantuono), Notes On Dialectics (James), Capital V I (Marx, Trans Reitter or Fowkes) and then returns to the present for The Future of Revolution (Bernes). 

If people agree the group will be run as a discussion by rotating facilitators. It could last 18 months or so.

title: Mark Kaplan, violin; Kyung Sun Lee, violin; Atar Arad, viola; Stephen Wyrczynski, viola; Brandon Vamos, cello
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  Beethoven: String Trio in E-Flat Major, Op. 3 (1796)W. A. Mozart: String Quintet in C Major, K.515About the Artists  Israeli-born violist and composer Atar Arad is distinguished professor of music in viola at the IU Jacobs School of Music. Summer activities include teaching at Keshet Eilon, Domaine Forget, Heifetz Institute, and, the Steans Music Institute. Cum laude first-prize winner at the Geneva International Music Competition (1972), he has performed worldwide in recitals and as a soloist with major orchestras and was a member of the celebrated Cleveland Quartet. Recordings with the quartet and as a soloist for such labels as Teldec, Telarc, RCA, and RIAX are widely acclaimed. His performance of Paganini's Sonata Per La Grand' Viola e Orchestra is considered a landmark in the history of the viola. Arad's compositions include a solo viola sonata, two string quartets, and more. Tikvah for viola solo was commissioned for the 2008 Munich International Viola Competition by ARD. Listen (Three Poems by W. S. Merwin) for tenor, clarinet, viola, cello, and bass was written for the International Musicians Seminar concert tour in England with Mark Padmore. Epitaph for cello and string orchestra was written for Gary Hoffman, who premiered it with the Kremerata Baltica Orchestra. Arad played the viola version at the 2012 International Viola Congress (IVC) and his 12 Caprices for Viola (Hofmeister Musikverlag) on concert tours of the United States, Canada, Israel, England, Germany, France, Spain, and Portugal. Recent performances include the Primrose Memorial Concert at Brigham Young University and a Toronto recital as the Lorand Fenyves Distinguished Visitor. At IVC 2018, he premiered Ceci n'est pas un Bach, a concerto for viola and strings. In June 2019, with Vadim Gluzman and Mark Kosower, he premiered his String Trio, commissioned by the North Shore Chamber Music Festival. He is a recipient of the American Viola Society's Career Achievement Award (June 2018); the International Viola Society's Silver Alto Clef 2018 ("in recognition for his outstanding contributions to the to the viola"); and the IU Trustees Teaching Award (2019). Arad plays on a viola by Niccolo Amati and uses PI strings by Thomastik.  A soloist of international distinction, violinist Mark Kaplan has performed with nearly every American, European, and Australian orchestra, and with many of the world's great conductors, including Ormandy, Rattle, Maazel, Masur, Dutoit, Salonen, Semkov, Skrowaczewski, and Tennstedt. He has made highly acclaimed concerto and recital appearances in all the musical centers of America and Europe, as well as in Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, Hong Kong, China and Singapore. Kaplan is also devoted to chamber music, appearing with pianist Yael Weiss and cellist Peter Stumpf as the Weiss-Kaplan-Stumpf Trio, with recordings and concert tours world-wide. Prior to that he performed and recorded extensively for two decades in the Golub-Kaplan-Carr Trio with cellist Colin Carr and the late pianist David Golub. Especially known for his interpretations of twentieth- and twenty-first-century works and the great German classics, his extensive discography of over 45 commercial CDs includes concertos, solo, and chamber works from Paganini, Bartk, Berg, Sarasate, and Nono to Schubert, Brahms, and Schumann, as well as two complete recordings of Bach's solo violin works. Since 2005, he has been professor of music in violin at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, following a decade as professor at UCLA. Kaplan is a graduate of The Juilliard School, where he studied with Dorothy DeLay.  Violinist Kyung Sun Lee is professor of music in violin at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. She captured a bronze medal in the 1993 Queen Elizabeth Competition, sixth prize in the 1994 Tchaikovsky Competition, first prizes at the Washington and D'Angelo International Competitions, and third prize in the Montreal International Competition, where she also won the Audience Favorite and Best Performance of the Commissioned Work prizes. Subsequent to winning these awards, Lee has enjoyed ever-increasing popularity as a performer and received high critical acclaim. The Strad praised her "exceptional tonal suavity and expressive intensity in equal measure," while Harris Goldsmith declared, "Godard's Concerto Romantique could not have had a more outstanding soloist than Kyung Sun Lee" (New York Concert Review Inc.). In addition to being in demand as a soloist and chamber musician, Lee is an accomplished teacher and clinician. After becoming assistant professor of violin at Oberlin Conservatory in fall 2001, then associate professor at the University of Houston in fall 2006, she has been professor at Seoul National University since 2009. Lee taught for two summers at the Aspen Music Festival and has also been on faculty at the Bowdoin Music Festival and the Heifetz International Institute. In recent, years she has been in demand as a judge of violin competitions including the Joachim International Violin Competition Hannover, Seoul International Competition, and Singapore International Violin Competition. She studied at Seoul National University, Peabody Conservatory, and The Juilliard School. Her teachers have included Sylvia Rosenberg, Robert Mann, and Dorothy Delay. Lee plays a Joseph Guarnerius violin from 1723 and is music director of Changwon International Chamber Music Festival and Seoul Virtuosi Chamber Orchestra.Brandon Vamos is professor of practice (cello) at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music and a member of the Pacifica Quartet, the school's faculty quartet in residence. Vamos has appeared as soloist with orchestras worldwide and has collaborated with many distinguished artists, including Paul Katz, Michael Tree, Yo-Yo Ma, Menahem Pressler, and the Emerson Quartet, and has recorded for Cedille, Naxos, and Cacophony Records. Awarded a Performer's Certificate at the Eastman School of Music, where he earned a Bachelor of Music degree as a student of Paul Katz, Vamos has also studied with distinguished artists such as Tanya Carey in Macomb, Illinois, and Aldo Parisot at Yale University, where he earned a Master of Music degree. As a member of the Pacifica Quartet, he won a 2009 Grammy Award for Best Chamber Music Performance and the Cleveland Quartet Award, in addition to being named Musical America's 2009 Ensemble of the Year.Stephen Wyrczynski is currently professor of music in viola at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. He was a member of the Philadelphia Orchestra for 18 years, joining them in 1992. Wyrczynski regularly performs as a soloist and chamber musician. He prioritizes faculty-student collaborations. One such partnership, which he cofounded with the late violinist Jorja Fleezanis, was an exploration of music from the Second Viennese School, in which faculty and students together performed music by Schoenberg, Webern, and Berg. Wyrczynski considers his teaching a direct result of his own relationship to performing, practicing, and listening. Teaching a student about the great privilege it is to serve the composers of our repertoire is one of the best ways for the students to gain ownership of their musical training. Most recently, he has completed a transcription of Igor Stravinsky's Rite of Spring with pianist Aram Arakelyan. Wyrczynski and Arakelyan gave the world premiere in the fall of 2024 and recorded it for Azica Records in the summer of 2025 with producer Alan Bise. A printed edition is published by Songburd Music. Wyrczynski will join the faculty of the Shepherd School of Music at Rice University in 2027.

title: Founders Exhibition - Frederick W. Rigley
description:
September 11 – November 1, 2026   

The Brown County Art Guild proudly presents the Founders Exhibition: Frederick W. Rigley, honoring one of the Guild’s founding artists and an important figure in the development of Brown County’s artistic legacy. Drawn from private collections, this exhibition brings together a rare selection of paintings that reflect Rigley’s deep appreciation for the landscapes, light, and character of southern Indiana. 

As a founding member of the Brown County Art Guild, Rigley helped establish an institution dedicated to preserving and promoting the artistic traditions of the region. His work captures the enduring beauty of Brown County while reflecting the values that shaped the early Guild—craftsmanship, observation, and a profound connection to place. 

By gathering these seldom-seen works, the exhibition offers visitors a unique opportunity to explore Rigley’s artistic contributions and gain a deeper understanding of the artists whose vision helped build one of Indiana’s most respected cultural organizations.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Chornobyl Never Ends: 40 Years Later
description: On April 26, 1986, the fourth reactor of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant exploded, marking one of the largest technological and environmental disasters of the twentieth century—a transnational, epidemiological, environmental, epistemological, and historiographical rupture.  The event had far-reaching consequences for global health policy, nuclear energy development, geopolitical power structures, and our understanding of knowledge, technology, and the environment. Yet Chornobyl never ends.  Chornobyl Never Ends returns to the discourse and experience of Chornobyl forty years after the disaster, looking beyond both the collapse of the Soviet Union and the post-Soviet period to consider its continuing significance in the wake of four years of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.  Oscillating between past, present, and future, the symposium asks what Chornobyl continues to mean—and what it makes visible—four decades later. How has the disaster shaped our understanding of technology, ecology, risk, memory, and political power? How have its meanings changed across different historical moments and political contexts? And what can the history of Chornobyl tell us about the uncertain nuclear futures ahead?  September 11, 2026  10 a.m. – Keynote lecture:  "Communist Technology, Rogue Operators, and a Dysfunctional Industry: Was Chernobyl an Accident Waiting to Happen?"  Sonja Schmid (U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission / Department of Science, Technology and Society, Virginia Tech)  Lecture abstract:  The world's worst catastrophe at a nuclear facility, the 1986 Chornobyl disaster, has alternately been blamed on a faulty reactor design, incompetent reactor personnel, or a deeply flawed economic system. This talk traces the extended "blame game" that ensued the accident and its mitigation and shows that neither of these factors alone caused the disaster. Rather, it argues, despite the general success of Soviet technology, the country's outstanding engineering education, and a dynamic managerial culture, Chornobyl was an accident of history: both deeply Soviet, and at the same time possible elsewhere.  Speaker's bio:  Sonja Schmid is a professor in the Department of Science, Technology, and Society at Virginia Tech (currently on leave), and the Historian at the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Her research is located at the interface of national energy policies, technological choices, and nonproliferation concerns. Her first book, Producing Power: The Pre‑Chernobyl History of the Soviet Nuclear Industry, was published by MIT Press in 2015. title: IKS Colloquium - Sue Hyon Bae
description: IKS Fall 2026 Colloquium Series  Sue Hyon Bae  Postdoctoral Fellow  Institute for Korean Studies  "Back to Nature: Traditional Medicine and Cancer Cures"Friday, September 1112:00-1:00pmGISB 2067 | 355 N Eagleson Ave  "South Korea has a long history of traditional medicine. Its foundational text, Hŏ Chun's Tongŭi Pogam, published under royal edict in 1613, is popularly cited today, and basic concepts adapted from traditional medicine, such as food as medicine and the superiority of local ingredients, are commonly practiced along with biomedicine. In this presentation, I analyze memoirs and self-help books that promote traditional Korean medicine (TKM) for the treatment of cancer. Written by diverse people, some practitioners of TKM and others patients, they share a common commitment to spreading an ideology, or a narrative about how illness is created and cured.  Although the details such as what kind of natural cure and the degree of faith they place in biomedicine differ, the TKM narratives ultimately argue that there is something wrong with the state of society. The TKM narratives also emphasize personal choice and control, showing a unique syncretization of modern and traditional medicine with neoliberal values. Many people, disillusioned not only with modern biomedicine but with modernity itself, turn to alternatives just as they would shop for different products in the belief they can buy health. What people blame for a disease that seems to have appeared out of nowhere, what they believe will cure them, and how traditional medicine is adapting itself to modernity even as it presents itself as a cure for modernity, is highly revealing about contemporary South Korean attitudes towards health, illness, and modern life."  Open to the public. A light lunch will be served.

title: American Foreign Policy in the Shadow of 9/11
description: Twenty-five years ago on 9/11, al-Qaeda terrorists attacked the United States, inflicting a death toll greater than Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor. The attacks delivered a profound shock to America's sense of security and place in the world and the international system. In response, the United States undertook a far-reaching "War on Terror"—the aftermath of which continues to influence our politics, national security, and the global balance of power. Counterterrorism, once a peripheral issue, quickly became the dominant policy priority. Washington launched large-scale and prolonged military interventions in Afghanistan, Iraq, and other crisis hotspots. Longstanding alliances were tested as new partnerships emerged. New forms of unmanned warfare were pioneered while national security agencies ballooned in size, budgets, and legal authorities. In short, 9/11 transformed American statecraft.  Join Professor of Practice Zachary Constantino for a moderated conversation with U.S. Ambassador (retired) Michael McKinley to unpack the wide-ranging impact the September 11 attacks had on American foreign policy. This will be an afternoon of reflection, assessing two decades of U.S. strategy and the legacy of those policies. Ambassador McKinley served for thirty-seven years in the U.S. Foreign Service, including as Ambassador to Afghanistan, Brazil, Peru, and Colombia. He also held senior diplomatic posts in Europe, Africa, and Washington, DC. Ambassador McKinley's experience on the front lines of diplomacy is extensive, encompassing efforts to advance peace negotiations in Colombia and Afghanistan to end conflict as well as successfully negotiating agreements to promote U.S. investment and market access. He is currently a senior counselor at The Cohen Group and a non-resident senior advisor with the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Ambassador McKinley is the author of numerous articles on foreign policy that have appeared in Foreign Affairs, Politico, The Washington Post, and other publications.  The IU Chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society is co-sponsoring this event.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.
